A.explanation: 250 J equals $100 \times 5.0 \times \sin 30^{\circ}$. This uses the vertical component of tension, which is perpendicular to the horizontal $5.0 \text{ m}$ displacement and does no work.

B.explanation: 290 J is too small and does not equal $100 \times 5.0 \times \cos 30^{\circ}$. The horizontal component is about $87 \text{ N}$, not about $58 \text{ N}$.

C.explanation: Work by an angled force is $F d \cos\theta = 100 \times 5.0 \times \cos 30^{\circ} \approx 433 \text{ J}$, which rounds to $430 \text{ J}$.

D.explanation: $500 \text{ J}$ equals $100 \times 5.0$ with no angle factor. This wrongly treats the full $100 \text{ N}$ tension as acting parallel to the horizontal surface.

hints: Notice the displacement is $5.0 \text{ m}$ along the horizontal surface, but the $100 \text{ N}$ tension in the diagram acts at $30^{\circ}$ above that direction.
Recall that only the component of force along the displacement does work, given by $W = F d \cos\theta$ where $\theta$ is the angle between force and displacement.
First work out the horizontal component $100 \cos 30^{\circ}$ in $\text{N}$, then multiply it by the $5.0 \text{ m}$ horizontal distance to get work in $\text{J}$.
walkthrough: Identify the given data from the text and diagram: force $F = 100 \text{ N}$, displacement $d = 5.0 \text{ m}$ horizontal, and angle between them $\theta = 30^{\circ}$.
State the rule for work done by a force at an angle to displacement: $W = F d \cos\theta$. Only $F\cos\theta$ acts along the motion.
Resolve the tension horizontally: $F_{horizontal} = F\cos 30^{\circ} = 100 \times \cos 30^{\circ} \approx 100 \times 0.866 = 86.6 \text{ N}$.
Multiply by distance: $W = 86.6 \times 5.0 \approx 433 \text{ J}$. Check units: $\text{N} \times \text{m} = \text{J}$.
To two significant figures this is $430 \text{ J}$, ignoring the $100\sin 30^{\circ}$ vertical component because there is no vertical displacement. This is option C.
